content: The LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, saying, {{v:2}} “This month shall be to you the beginning of months. It shall be the first month of the year to you. {{v:3}} Speak to all the congregation of Israel, saying, ‘On the tenth day of this month, they shall take to them every man a lamb, according to their fathers’ houses, a lamb for a household; {{v:4}} and if the household is too little for a lamb, then he and his neighbor next to his house shall take one according to the number of the souls. You shall make your count for the lamb according to what everyone can eat. {{v:5}} Your lamb shall be without defect, a male a year old. You shall take it from the sheep or from the goats. {{v:6}} You shall keep it until the fourteenth day of the same month; and the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall kill it at evening. {{v:7}} They shall take some of the blood, and put it on the two door posts and on the lintel, on the houses in which they shall eat it. {{v:8}} They shall eat the meat in that night, roasted with fire, with unleavened bread. They shall eat it with bitter herbs. {{v:9}} Don’t eat it raw, nor boiled at all with water, but roasted with fire; with its head, its legs and its inner parts. {{v:10}} You shall let nothing of it remain until the morning; but that which remains of it until the morning you shall burn with fire. {{v:11}} This is how you shall eat it: with your belt on your waist, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and you shall eat it in haste: it is the LORD’s Passover. {{v:12}} For I will go through the land of Egypt in that night, and will strike all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, both man and animal. I will execute judgments against all the gods of Egypt. I am the LORD. {{v:13}} The blood shall be to you for a token on the houses where you are. When I see the blood, I will pass over you, and no plague will be on you to destroy you when I strike the land of Egypt.

facets.text: The institution of Passover reorders Israel's very calendar, making the month of deliverance 'the beginning of months' and the first month of the year. Time itself is reconstituted around God's saving act, so that the nation's history is measured from redemption. This teaches that liberation from bondage is the foundational event that gives Israel its identity and orients all its life toward the LORD.
facets.question: Why does God make the month of the Passover the beginning of the year for Israel?

facets.text: The lamb must be without defect, a male a year old, kept from the tenth day and slain by the whole assembly at evening on the fourteenth. The Church reads this spotless victim as a figure of Christ, the 'Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world' (John 1:29), the true Passover sacrificed for us (1 Cor 5:7). John notes that not one of the lamb's bones was to be broken, fulfilled when Christ's legs were not broken on the cross (John 19:36).
facets.question: How does the unblemished Passover lamb prefigure Jesus Christ?

facets.text: Salvation comes through the blood placed on the doorposts and lintel: when the LORD sees the blood, he passes over that house and no destroying plague touches it. The blood is a 'token' that shields the household from judgment, prefiguring the saving power of the Blood of Christ, by which the faithful are marked and delivered from death. Redemption is not earned but received under the sign of sacrificial blood.
facets.question: What is the meaning of the blood on the doorposts that causes God to pass over?

facets.text: The lamb is not merely slain but eaten—roasted whole, with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, nothing left until morning. The saving sacrifice becomes a communal meal that must be consumed, uniting the household to the victim whose blood protects them. Catholic tradition sees here a foreshadowing of the Eucharist, where the paschal Lamb who is sacrificed is also given as food to those he saves.
facets.question: Why must the Passover lamb be eaten and not merely sacrificed?

facets.text: The meal is eaten in haste—belt fastened, sandals on the feet, staff in hand—as a people already on the move toward freedom. The Passover is inseparable from the Exodus journey; those saved by the blood are those who set out from Egypt. This pilgrim posture teaches that redemption summons the redeemed to leave bondage behind and journey toward the promise.
facets.question: Why did the Israelites eat the Passover dressed and ready to depart in haste?

facets.text: God declares he will strike the firstborn and 'execute judgments against all the gods of Egypt,' concluding with 'I am the LORD.' The Passover is thus an act of divine sovereignty over false gods and oppressive powers, vindicating the LORD as the one true God who alone delivers. Salvation history advances through God's decisive victory over every idol that enslaves.
facets.question: What does it mean that God executes judgment against the gods of Egypt at the Passover?

facets.text: The rite is given to 'all the congregation of Israel,' arranged household by household, with a lamb shared among neighbors when a family is too small. Redemption is enacted within the covenant community and its domestic bonds, not in isolation. The whole assembly acts together, prefiguring the ecclesial dimension of salvation in which the people of God are saved as a body.
facets.question: Why is the Passover celebrated by households and the whole congregation together?

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: The institution of the Passover in Egypt (Exodus 12:1–13): the calendar of deliverance, the unblemished lamb, the saving blood on the doorposts, the sacred meal eaten in pilgrim haste, God's judgment over Egypt's gods, and the communal covenantal character of redemption. Rich with Christological and Eucharistic typology.

[SCRIPTURAL | explicit]: God resets Israel's calendar so the month of deliverance becomes the first month, making redemption the foundation of national identity and time.
[TYPOLOGICAL | traditional]: The spotless year-old male lamb prefigures Christ, the Lamb of God and true Passover, with the unbroken bones fulfilled on the cross (John 19:36).
[TYPOLOGICAL | traditional]: The blood on doorposts and lintel is the saving token that averts judgment, foreshadowing the redeeming Blood of Christ.
[TYPOLOGICAL | traditional]: The sacrificed lamb must also be eaten as a household meal, prefiguring the Eucharist where the paschal Lamb is both offered and given as food.
[DEVOTIONAL | inferential]: The meal eaten in haste with belt, sandals, and staff marks the redeemed as pilgrims summoned to leave bondage and journey to the promise.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: God strikes Egypt's firstborn and judges all its gods, declaring 'I am the LORD,' revealing Passover as divine victory over idols and oppressive powers.
[DOCTRINAL | inferential]: Redemption is enacted household by household within the whole congregation, showing the communal and ecclesial character of salvation.
